title: The Hare That Turns First
creature: A hare who goes white a week before the snow
summary: The village plants by the hare, not by the calendar. This year the hare turned in October.

chapters.title: Seven Days
chapters.text: The hare turned white seven days before the snow, every year, and had done for longer than anybody could account for. This was not a story in Bjørnstad. It was not told at parties or written on anything. It was the sort of fact that a place keeps in the same drawer as the date the water gets turned off and which side of the church the ice comes in on — dull, useful, and known by everybody in a way that meant nobody explained it. The hare lived on the slope above the last houses. There was only ever one. When one died another was there the following spring, which people accepted without much comment, in the way you accept that there is always a robin in the churchyard. And in October or November — it moved about, which was the whole point of the thing — the hare would come down onto the lower ground one morning with its coat gone from brown to white, and everybody in the village would look at it and go home and do the seven days' work. The seven days' work was specific. You brought the outside animals down. You lifted whatever was still in the ground, potatoes especially, because potatoes in frozen ground are potatoes you have lost. You got the winter wood stacked under the eave and not merely stacked. You put the boards over the pump. You did the thing with the pipe under the Hansens' bridge that nobody could explain the reason for but which had been done every year since 1938 and which the year it was not done, in 1971, had cost the village a great deal of money. Seven days was exactly enough time if you started on the first day. Marit's grandfather had done the sums once, on the back of a feed bag, in about 1980, and the feed bag had been kept. Two people, seven days, working evenings and the whole of a weekend, came out at just over the total. Not comfortably over. Over by about half a day, which meant that a broken pump or a sick cow or somebody's back going ate the margin entirely. That was why the seven days was a village thing and not a household thing. Nobody in Bjørnstad got their own potatoes up. Everybody got everybody's potatoes up, in a rolling order that had been settled some time before the war and that was never discussed, and if you were new you were told the order once and then never again. The Hansens went first because they were oldest. The top houses went last because they had the pump and the pump had to be done anyway. You did not thank anyone. Marit had once, at nine, thanked Kristian's mother for coming, and had been looked at in a way that stopped her doing it again. It was not enough time if you started on the third. The year they started on the third was 1971, and it is the only year anybody in Bjørnstad ever refers to by its number. What happened in 1971 was not dramatic and that is exactly why it is remembered. The hare turned on the ninth of November. A man called Sverre, who had come from Bergen two years earlier and who was by all accounts perfectly capable, was at that time renting the mill house and had responsibility for the stretch of pipe under the Hansens' bridge. He did not do the thing with the pipe. He did not refuse to do it. He simply did not know it was his, because the man who had told him the order had told him once, at a wedding, and had not mentioned the pipe, because the pipe was not part of the order — the pipe was just a thing the mill house did. The pipe froze and split on the second night of the snow and the water went under the Hansens' bridge instead of through it, and the bridge came off its abutment in the January thaw, and the village was seventeen months and a great deal of money getting a new one. Nobody blamed Sverre. Marit has checked this with three separate people who were adults at the time and they all say the same thing with some force: nobody blamed Sverre, Sverre was fine, Sverre was told wrong. What the village blamed was the telling. And from 1972 there was a list, typed, on the wall of the co-op, with everything on it including the pipe, and it is still there, and it has been retyped twice.

chapters.title: The Hare Was Wrong
chapters.text: Marit was twelve the year the hare turned in the second week of October, which was three weeks early and which nobody at all had been expecting. She saw it first, from the school bus, which she was extremely pleased about for approximately four hours. By the evening she understood that being first to see it had put her in the middle of the only argument the village had had in seventeen years. Because the hare, that year, was wrong. Everybody could see it was wrong. The birches still had most of their leaves and the leaves were still half green. There had not been a frost. The forecast — and Bjørnstad had had a proper forecast on a phone for about a decade by then, which is important to this — the forecast said mild and wet for the whole of the following fortnight, and then more mild and wet, and the long-range said a late winter. Her father said the hare had got it wrong and that was all there was to it. Her mother said the hare had never once got it wrong. Her father said that a thing that has not got something wrong yet has still only not got it wrong yet, and that he was not lifting two hundred kilos of potatoes in the second week of October on the say-so of a rabbit. Her mother said it was a hare. Marit went out to the woodpile, which is what you did in that house when the kitchen got like that. She split wood for forty minutes, badly, and thought about it. The thing that bothered her was not that her father might be wrong. Her father was wrong about plenty of things and said so, eventually, in his own time. What bothered her was that he had a reason and her mother did not. Her father could say: here is the forecast, here is where it comes from, here are the satellites, here is a man on the television with a map. Her mother could say: the hare has never been wrong. And Marit could see, standing in the cold with the axe, that those two sentences were not the same kind of sentence at all, and that everybody in the village was about to have to choose between them, and that the choosing was going to be based on something other than which one was true. She went in at nine and her parents were being polite to each other, which was worse.

chapters.title: The Village Split
chapters.text: What happened over the next three days was, Marit thinks now, the most interesting thing she has ever watched, and at the time she mostly found it embarrassing. The village split, and it did not split the way you would expect. It did not split old against young. That was the thing that surprised her. The Hansens, who were both over seventy, looked at the forecast and did nothing. Kristian at the garage, who was twenty-six and had a tattoo of a wolf and who nobody would have picked, brought his mother's sheep down on the first afternoon and said, when asked, that his grandfather had been very clear with him about the hare and that he was not going to be the one who tested it. It did not split by belief either. Nobody in the village believed the hare was magic. Marit asked several people directly, in the blunt way you can at twelve, and got six versions of the same answer: it is a hare, it goes white when it goes white, there is presumably a reason, the reason is presumably to do with light or cold or something in the ground. The split was about something else, and it took her until she was much older to put a name on it. She watched it happen over three days at the co-op, which was the only shop and therefore the whole of public life. People came in and bought things, and what they bought told you where they stood. Sacks. Twine. The particular blue tarpaulin. Batteries, which was the tell, because batteries in the second week of October means somebody is expecting the power to go. Nobody argued in the shop. That was not how it was done. What happened instead was that two people would meet at the till and one of them would have twine and the other would not, and there would be a fractional pause, and then they would talk about something else with great warmth for four minutes. By the Wednesday the shop had run out of twine and had not run out of anything else, which told you the proportion better than any conversation. Marit's mother did the seven days' work alone, in the evenings, without ever once asking Marit's father to help. Marit helped. She wants that recorded too, because at the time she told herself she was helping her mother and she has since worked out that she was hedging, and that hedging is the most common position in any argument of this kind and the one nobody ever admits to. It was between the people who trusted a thing they could not explain because it had never failed, and the people who trusted a thing they could explain because they could explain it. Her father was firmly in the second group and made an excellent case at every meal. About half the village did the seven days' work. The other half looked at the sky, which was mild, and at the leaves, which were on the trees, and got on with October.

chapters.title: The Twenty-Second
chapters.text: The snow came on the night of the twenty-second, which was nine days after the hare turned, and it did not stop for four days. It was not a normal fall. That has to be said, because otherwise the story sounds smug and it was not smug at the time; it was frightening. Two metres came down onto ground that was not frozen, which meant the whole lot sat there wet and enormously heavy, and the power went at some point on the second night, and the road out was not cleared until the twenty-eighth. Nobody was hurt. Marit wants that first. Nobody in Bjørnstad was hurt, that year or any year, and the village is still there and so is most of what happened to it. But the Hansens lost their long greenhouse, which went in under the weight on the second night with a noise she heard from her bedroom. Four houses at the top lost water for fourteen days because the pump was not boarded. The Iversens' potatoes were still in the ground and stayed in the ground and came up in April as a smell. And on the third morning, in a whiteout, with the power off, Kristian from the garage went out on the tractor and got as far as the top houses, because his tractor had a blade on it, because he had put the blade on it on the fourteenth of October when the forecast said mild. Marit's father did not say anything about the hare that winter. He did not admit anything either — that is not how he was made — and the two of them never had a conversation where he said *you were right* or *the hare was right*, because that was not available in that house. What he did was this. The following autumn, on the morning the hare turned, which that year was the fourth of November and entirely reasonable, Marit came downstairs at half past six and her father was already dressed and had the box of potato sacks out on the table. He said, "It's turned, then." And she said, "Yes." And he said, "Right," and went out. She has thought about that a great deal since, because she works in meteorology now, which several people in the village find extremely funny. She has run the numbers on it. She has the records — the parish kept the date of the turning and the date of the first snow going back to 1911, in a ledger, because of course they did — and she has done the arithmetic properly, with error bars, twice, as an adult who is paid to do exactly this. The gap is seven days, plus or minus two, for a hundred and fourteen years. She has no explanation. There are three or four candidates and none of them survives contact with the data, and she has written about it once, carefully, in a journal that six people read. What she says, when people ask her at conferences, is that she does not know how the hare does it and that this has never once been the interesting part. The interesting part is that her village had a hundred and fourteen years of a signal that worked, and a mild October, and a forecast on a phone, and that half of them looked at all three of those things and picked the one that came with an explanation.
